textos.1: Three centuries ago, when the world still trembled with prayers, a showman in a black cape climbed up to the Miracle every spring with cages of birds that sang in human voices: the Birdcatcher. The children who listened to him lost their laughter forever.
textos.2: Shepherds and monks rose up against him and locked him in his own cage, deep down in the earth. The monks sealed the iron door with the light of the sword of the Miracle, Runna. They left it to sleep among the stones, waiting for the day the darkness would return.
textos.3: But the darkness does not forget. Three nights ago, a cold violet mist rose from under the ground: it withers the gardens, clouds the waters and has silenced the sacred organ of the Sanctuary.
textos.4: And every night, the mist claims a child. / An empty bed in Sant Benet, and then another. / And on this cursed night... a third cradle has gone cold.
textos.5: When dawn sets the sky of the Miracle ablaze once more, a young monk wakes up in the Monastery: Ineu. / Fate has chosen him, though he does not know it. Father Jòrdius is waiting for him in the Square.
textos.6: Ineu! What are you doing on the ground? Breathe, son! You'll hurt yourself. Are you all right now?
textos.7: Another night of mist... and this cold that won't go away. Father Jòrdius must be waiting for me in the Square.

textos.9: Ineu, good morning. I'm glad you're up, I was looking for you.
textos.10: I don't want to scare you. For three nights a violet mist has been rising from under the ground, and every night a child goes missing: Huri and Fram, from the cells of Sant Benet, next door to each other; and tonight, Sardi, the ward of the priestesses of the Guesthouse.
textos.11: Nobody saw them leave. The beds are unmade, and the windows locked from the inside. All that's left is a smell of wet earth.
textos.12: You have good eyes and a good heart. Talk to everyone and tell me everything. Be careful on the paths, Ineu.
textos.13: Ineu! I heard: the Linden has given you its permission. That tree doesn't give it to just anyone.
textos.14: Listen, son: I'm not brave like you, but I do know one thing. A blessing isn't a magic word, it's true goodwill. Bow your head.
textos.15: You're not alone, Ineu. The whole Miracle is with you.
textos.16: And take this. It's a stone medallion, carved with an open hand, kept by every generation of priors of the Miracle. Now it must be yours: take it to the Dolmen.
textos.17: ★ You got the MEDALLION OF THE BLESSING!
textos.18: Ineu, people say you've spoken with the Great Linden. To awaken Runna you need three things: the tree's permission (its medallion), the Words of Wisdom of Father Alberic and my blessing.
textos.20: The critters have come out onto the paths, Ineu. Even some visitors, who came up to the Miracle to take photos, are wandering about with greenish skin and a lost look: the mist has muddled them and they don't even know who they are. If you see any in the Sanctuary or the Cemetery, don't be afraid.
textos.21: They're not bad, poor things: just put them to sleep and they'll wake up remembering nothing. When the mist goes away, they'll be tourists again.
textos.23: Talk to people: the families in the cells, the brothers, the Pianist... Someone must have seen something.
textos.24: If you get lost, the Venerable Wise Women of the cells always have good advice.

← Big House
↓ The Bassadòria
textos.26: Ineu! What a fuss, eh? Everyone running up and down... I bet the children are just hiding to play.
textos.27: Are you a Barça fan? I've got some trading cards the children are dying to have. They listen to me, at least.
textos.28: I've got this pilgrim's staff. It's dangerous to go alone. Take it.
textos.30: I don't have time today, Ineu. I have... things to do.
textos.31: Hey, can't you hear something? Like a tiny little voice calling me from under the ground... Must be the wind. Força Barça!
textos.32: The flowers at the foot of the cross have straightened up. Now that the water is clear again, they've got their colour back too.
textos.33: Today the flowers are wilted. As if the mist were drinking their colour.
textos.34: And one more thing: Rosansa, the vegetable seller, has come by the cells again with her cart. If you're ever looking for a strange seed, you know who to ask.
textos.35: Shall we try again, son? Listen carefully to the notes.
textos.36: Oh, Ineu, son... Come in, come in. Forgive me for not looking at you, I can't leave the organ.
textos.37: I've played every day for forty years and the sound had never failed me. Now my fingers move over the keys, but not a single note comes out of the organ.
textos.38: Since the mist came, three nights ago, the Sanctuary has fallen silent. I'm afraid it's swallowing all the music.
textos.39: But there's one song the mist can't swallow: the Song of Dawn. Only you have nothing to play it on.
textos.40: Let me tell you where this comes from. Many years ago, the Cortiner played the music for the Sanctuary's performances, and he had a tarota.
textos.41: He used to say the curtains that really matter aren't made of velvet, but of mist, brambles and stones, and that the right notes can draw them aside.
textos.42: I never managed to make it sound like he did. Take it, son: maybe it will obey you.
textos.44: A monk's shadow in the Ruins says you know a song the stones understand.
textos.45: The shepherds of the Cirosa haven't heard music by the fire in years. The Great Linden says you keep a song as old as they are.
textos.46: A song the stones understand? Oh, son... Maybe it's the Vespers Song: it's very old, my mother taught it to me. Come, listen.
textos.47: A song as old as they are? I have the Vespers Song, son: very old, my mother taught it to me. Maybe it will remind them of home. Come, listen.
textos.48: Oh, Ineu, son, you're carrying Runna! I can see it in your eyes. Then I must teach you the last song, the one the Birdcatcher stole from the birds: the Song of the Miracle.
textos.49: I remember it because my mother used to sing it. Listen to me and repeat what I play. Learn it well: you'll need it down there.
textos.52: The Bassadòria is clean now, son. You did it. Come and see me again when you have another song to learn.
textos.53: If you find a way to bring the music back, bring it to me. I'm not moving from this bench, even if the world ends. Play the song on the tarota when you're in the right place.
textos.54: Did you hear the organ? The D still falters, but it sings. Listen.
textos.55: And you, son, never leave the tarota in a drawer.
textos.56: That's it, that's it! You've got an ear, son. The Song of Dawn: three notes, and the mist draws back.
textos.57: Take this tarota. It belonged to the Cortiner, the musician who played for the Sanctuary's performances. He used to say the most important curtains weren't made of velvet.
textos.58: Mist, brambles and stones are veils too: the right notes can wake what they hide. I never managed to make it sound like he did. Maybe it will listen to you.
textos.60: Play it in front of the water of the Bassadòria, the water that comes out murky. That's where the mist has its root.
textos.61: The Vespers Song: 5-4-3-1. If that monk is waiting for it, play it in front of him: the old stones have always understood it.
textos.62: The Vespers Song: 5-4-3-1. Play it by the shepherds' fire: such an old song might remind them of home.
textos.63: The Vespers Song: 5-4-3-1. It's very old: the old stones have always understood it.
textos.64: That's it, son! The Song of the Miracle. The birds used to sing it at dawn, before the Birdcatcher took it and locked it in his cage.
textos.65: My mother says that cage only opens with the song that was stolen from the birds. If the children are inside, play it in front of the bars and they'll have no choice but to open.
textos.66: Father Nadiel, the parchment I found in the Ruins says the other half is in the tabernacle. Do you know where the key is?
textos.67: The tabernacle? I keep a few old papers of the monks in there, so the damp doesn't eat them. If Father Alberic is looking for them, it's about time someone read them!
textos.68: But the key, oh, I haven't known where it is for years: a small one, like a toy. The old monks used to leave their things at the hermitage of the Disappearance. Maybe it's there.
textos.69: Ineu! How good to see you! Come, I need new voices for the choir.
textos.70: The Pianist and I have been friends all our lives. She plays like no one else, and I lead the singing. But the music has lost its organ, as you can see.
textos.71: Don't worry: if the music has hidden away, we'll sing it back! Laughter is the first prayer.
textos.72: Oh, and something that worries me: the tower clock stopped at a quarter past three, the night the mist came.
textos.73: The door to the right of the altarpiece goes up the tower to the Clock Room, but it's locked, and Carry, the clockmaker's widow, keeps the key at Our Lady's. My back can't manage all those steps any more, but you... go and see what's wrong.
textos.75: The Clock Room, son: the door to the right of the altarpiece, and up the tower. If someone gets it ticking again, maybe the mist will think twice.
textos.76: The door to the right of the altarpiece is locked, son: Carry, the clockmaker's widow, keeps the key at Our Lady's. If someone gets the clock ticking, maybe the mist will think twice.
textos.77: Can you hear the clock, Ineu? It's ticking again! I hadn't heard it for three nights. The children tell me I sing too loudly, but today there's no need: it does it for me!
textos.78: And now that time is moving again, let me tell you something people told me while it was stopped:
textos.79: And now that time is moving again...
textos.82: "Stones keep what they are told. Whoever stays silent long enough will hear them answer."
textos.83: (This stone doesn't match the rest of the wall. I put my ear to it and it seems to be listening... Maybe it wants to hear the Vespers Song.)
textos.84: (This stone doesn't match the rest of the wall. I put my ear to it and it seems to be listening... but I don't know what it wants to hear.)
textos.85: A passage between the Monastery and the Sanctuary! The old monks really knew how to hide things.
textos.86: "For the one who knows how to listen to stones."
textos.87: The tabernacle is locked with a very small key.
textos.89: Fragment 2 of 2: / "The monk guarded the seal until his last day. Since then his shadow returns every night to the wall of the Ruins to keep watch. The iron key is where he left it, with his brothers, under the gaze of a stone guardian."
textos.90: "Whoever seeks the key must never forget where the sun is born."
textos.91: The clock tower key fits the lock. The door opens.
textos.93: The water is clean now: clear and calm again, and the violet mist has faded away.
textos.94: The water has always been clear... Now it's murky and smells of cellars. And these poisonous toads come out of it, along with puffs of violet mist.
textos.96: It worked! The water is clean...
textos.97: It worked! The water in the basin is clear as glass again.
textos.98: ★ You got the WATER OF THE BISHOP'S FOUNTAIN.
textos.99: The Venerable Wise Women say that on Midsummer's Night this water could heal. Now it's dead... There are letters carved on the basin: "St John's wort, rialla and the fruit of the golden tree."
textos.100: Rialla... It's not a laugh at all: it's a PLANT! The Venerable Wise Women spoke of a flower that grows surrounded by poisonous mushrooms, in the Wood of the Pine of the Three Songs.
textos.101: St John's wort glows, always in a clearing: there must be some around here, in this very wood. And the golden tree... it's the Magic Plum Tree, in the Guesthouse garden! A plum.
textos.102: Hey! You! Who the dickens said you could come in? You friars never come round here! Clear off or I'll make mushrooms grow in your ears!
textos.103: Sorry... I came through the oak. I've brought water from the Bishop's Fountain.
textos.104: Water... from the Bishop's Fountain?! Give me thaaat! I haven't had a single clean drop in thirty years.
textos.105: Mmm... cracking. You're daft, lad, but you're good. The birds and the foxes chatter, and I hear everything: you're looking for the Great Linden, aren't you? They've blocked the path to it with a mist the wind won't carry off.
textos.106: Look, I've mixed the water that's left with rialla, St John's wort and a bit of golden plum. This brew chases off the bad mist. Don't drink it, mind! Just pour it on the mist, or you'll sprout mushrooms.
textos.109: Now clear off, I've got soup to see to. And don't tell anyone where I live, or I'll turn you into a mushroom.
textos.110: The pot isn't bubbling purple any more. Now it smells of thyme, as it should.
textos.111: I've brought water from the Bishop's Fountain. Maybe...
textos.112: ...Who brings us... the good... water... Come in, come in, child... Only Joaneta... knows where you'll end up.
textos.113: I can hear a voice in there... "Water... water from the Bishop's Fountain..." Maybe I need the water from the fountain nearby.
textos.114: Sant Joan Wood. / "Whoever seeks the fountain, follow the water... and whoever doesn't, don't get lost."
textos.115: "For whoever gets lost on the way and finds it."

textos.119: Don't stuff yourself, monk! They're golden plums, magic ones: just one leaves you as good as new. My Sardi used to eat ten every afternoon and it was never enough...
textos.122: It worked! The path to the Great Linden is clear again.
textos.123: I can't get through. This mist isn't the kind the wind blows away: to clear it I'd need some liquid, a potion... something I don't have.
textos.124: Three hundred years ago I saw that cage go down into the darkness, little monk. And since then I have never closed my eyes.
textos.125: Now I feel the earth cracking beneath my roots. The old cemeteries are opening, and everything that slept in them is coming out: and it means no good.
textos.126: Your pilgrim's staff is good for a quiet road. This one no longer is. Raise your eyes, little monk.
textos.127: A branch of mine, strengthened by three centuries of wind and sorrow. Take it: it will be nimbler and more alive than any staff.
textos.128: The tree that gives a branch does not die. It grew for this day: may it guard you as it has guarded me.
textos.129: The branch is on the ground, near my roots. Take it, little monk.
textos.130: The permission is yours, little monk, and the candles are still lit. Remember at the table those who are missing.
textos.131: The permission is yours, little monk, and the candles are still lit. Remember at the table those who are missing. May Runna rest lightly in your hand.
textos.133: I hear the water singing far away... The Bassadòria is clean. You did well, little monk.
textos.134: I closed the north-east path to the Cirosa with my roots, so the mist wouldn't climb up. Now that the water breathes, you can pass: the roots only recognise my branch. Strike them with it and they'll sink into the ground.
textos.135: In the Cirosa live some exiled shepherds who keep their grandparents' cowbells: the ancient songs were tuned with them. Treat them gently, they have suffered enough.
textos.136: And be careful: Brother Aleu goes up there at night by a pass I don't watch, and he carries the mist inside him. The Man in the Cage whispers in his ear, and he listens.
textos.137: I will give you my permission when you have brought life back to the land the mist has sickened. You have restored the water: the land still remains.
textos.139: These are the roots of the Great Linden. The pilgrim's staff won't move them... but maybe they'd recognise a branch from the same tree.
textos.140: The roots shivered when they recognised the branch, but they won't sink. They seem to be waiting for something: maybe for the clear water of the Bassadòria to breathe again.
textos.141: ↑ The Cirosa (long way, uphill all the way) / ← The Hut / ↓ The Cells
textos.143: They sat me at the table... They passed me the bread. No one had passed me the bread in fifty years.
textos.144: The flock is back in the pen. I don't know how to thank you, monk. All we want is a little peace, and a corner where nobody looks at us badly.
textos.145: Don't come too close, Father, people say we bring bad luck. All we have is the flock... and Brother Aleu, that tiresome monk who was always playing with the children, has taken it from us. Now he calls himself the Shepherd of the Mist.
textos.146: There were flowers on the table. It had been so long since I'd seen flowers on a table.
textos.147: We had land on the plain, and wells, and a house with a hearth. We lost it all, and the village turned its back on us. Up here, at least, nobody avoids us.
textos.148: We do no harm to anyone. We're just trying to rebuild what we have left.
textos.149: Son, Brother Aleu put on a kind face, but he already carried that inside him. The Birdcatcher, the Man in the Cage, only promised him that everyone would follow him, and he believed it.
textos.150: And not just the sheep. A few nights ago we saw him going down towards the village with a sleeping child in his arms. The missing children, son, he's the one who took them.
textos.151: Our grandparents locked that cage underground centuries ago, and the village repaid us with forgetting.
textos.152: If you find a way to take that thing out of him, we'll be grateful. There are some cowbells that belonged to our grandparents: we'll give them to you, but the flock is in the pasture, and he's there.
textos.153: You've brought back the flock. Brother Aleu went off down the path laughing: he still carries the mist inside him, poor man. God bless you for it, monk.
textos.154: Here are our grandparents' cowbells. Let them ring with your tarota, and may the ancient songs guide you.
textos.156: We cried at the table, monk. We cried like children. May the tree bless you all, even those of us who have no name.
textos.157: A supper, you say? At the Linden? With the people from the cells?... No, son. We're not the sort of folk who sit down with folk.
textos.158: It's been years since we heard music by the fire, or kneaded the bread we used to make for feast days. If someone played... maybe it would remind us that we're still people.
textos.159: I have the tarota. Their grandparents' cowbells tuned the ancient songs... The Vespers Song: I'll play it by the fire, and God's will be done.
textos.160: I have the tarota, but I only know a few songs. The old folk know them all: maybe the Pianist, at the Sanctuary, knows one that will remind them of home.
textos.161: This pasture is a peaceful place again. Thank you for that.
textos.162: The sheep are white again. One or two still have slightly purple ears, but it'll pass.
textos.164: No one has invited us anywhere in fifty years, monk. Not to a mass, not to a table. And you speak to us with music.
textos.165: Look: the oven is still warm. We kneaded this bread ourselves, with these hands, like before. Take it to your tree. And we'll come, we won't say much, but the bread will speak for us.
textos.167: (The fire crackles and the shepherds are silent. An ancient song by the embers, the Vespers Song, might open their hearts...)
textos.168: (The fire crackles and the shepherds are silent. Some old music by the embers might open their hearts... Maybe the Pianist, at the Sanctuary, knows some.)
textos.169: (For those who have no name. Someone remembered them.)
textos.170: "The Birdcatcher came down every spring with his caged birds. The children laughed with them; afterwards they laughed at nothing at all. There were years of weeping in the houses."
textos.171: "We shepherds and monks locked him in his cage, underground, and a monk sealed the door with the light of the sword. The village was happy for three days. Then it wanted someone to blame, and it blamed us."
textos.172: "Whoever finds this, do not forget us: we opened our eyes before anyone else. We only did what had to be done."
textos.173: (The old shepherd has them. I need to talk to him by the fire.)
textos.174: (Who knows where they are now. Maybe the shepherds keep them.)
textos.177: Aleu was a monk nobody ever looked at. Now I'm the Shepherd of the Mist. Look at them, how they follow me. No one had ever followed me before.
textos.178: Ever since the mist rose, a voice speaks inside my head, softly, just for me. It saw me when no one else did. It's the voice of the Master.
textos.179: A voice inside your head... Aleu, it's the Man in the Cage. The Birdcatcher is speaking through your mouth.
textos.180: The Man in the Cage, yes! The Master promised me: "All who are afraid will follow you." And now I'm his shepherd. The SHEPHERD OF THE MIST!
textos.181: Where are Huri, Fram and Sardi?
textos.182: They're asleep. I took them to the Master myself, one by one, at night. In there they're not afraid of anything any more.
textos.183: Aleu, the thing that talks to you isn't good. You can still turn back.
textos.184: Turn back? Never! The Master saw me, when no one else did. Be quiet! Baa-a-a!
textos.185: You've won this one, monk... For thirty years no one looked at me, and he did. I'll never let him down.
textos.186: The Master is at the bottom of the Gírgoles, and he's already awake: his voice calls me from down there and never stops. Come, if you dare: the children are already his, and I'm only the first of his birds.
textos.187: Heh, heh, heh... See you down there, monk.
textos.188: ("At the bottom of the Gírgoles"... Now I know where to look.)
textos.189: (And the old shepherd promised me his grandparents' cowbells. I'll go and see him by the fire.)
textos.190: You've brought music to a place that hadn't had any for years. It makes me think of the supper.
textos.191: Once a year, in autumn, the people of the cells sit beneath my branches and eat together. You call it the Linden supper. I don't eat, but I listen. All the wisdom of a tree is listening to people eating together.
textos.192: This year nobody feels like sitting at table: three empty chairs, and the village afraid. The mist feeds on loneliness, little monk. And half measures won't do: the table must be full.
textos.193: Three hundred years ago, when they closed the cage, the shepherds of the Cirosa sat here with the monks and the pilgrims. Then they were driven out, and people forgot they belonged here too. Let food come from every home, theirs too. And let there be flowers.
textos.194: Bring Nelis's escudella stew, Isílder's flowers and the bread the shepherds of the Cirosa knead with their own hands. Then, and only then, will I give you my permission.
textos.195: But the shepherds won't sit at the table for words alone: they haven't heard music by the fire for years. Before you go back, go and see the Pianist at the Sanctuary: she keeps a song as old as they are.
textos.196: The table isn't full yet, little monk. Eating alone is merely feeding yourself; that's why we must all be there.
textos.197: You've brought everything. Let the supper begin.
textos.198: This year the escudella tastes of little, son: it's missing the joy of three children. May all three forgive us, wherever they are.
textos.199: I've put the moon flowers in the middle, like every year. This time they're for Huri, for Fram... and for my Sardi.
textos.200: We always do the same, son: a candle for every empty chair at the table. This year there are three: Huri, Fram and Sardi. You light them: you're the one we've put our hopes in.
textos.201: It's been many years since anyone kept a chair for us at any table. Thank you for inviting us, son.
textos.202: This is the wisdom I wanted to give you, little monk: no one is wholly lost while someone remembers them at the table. The Birdcatcher's cage is filled only with those who have been left alone.
textos.203: Receive my permission. May it rest lightly on you, and may it never let you forget that you ate with everyone.
textos.204: Among my branches I have kept, since time immemorial, a stone medallion carved with a leaf: the tree's permission. For centuries it has waited for someone who would sit at the table with everyone. Take it.
textos.205: ★ You got the MEDALLION OF THE TREE!
textos.206: (They look like plans for some kind of device for looking at the stars.)
textos.207: The Linden supper? Oh, Ineu, who feels like sitting at table this year! With three children missing...
textos.208: ...But the Linden is right, curse it. You can't stop doing what's always been done, not even when your heart aches. Take the escudella, and don't spill it!
textos.209: It's the same escudella as every year, our grandmothers' recipe, but this year it has a taste I'd rather not explain. You make sure you carry it there whole.
textos.211: Ineu, son, don't just stand there! Huri and Fram slept right here, in Sant Benet, next door to each other, and now they're gone. And nobody's doing anything!
textos.213: You hush, you're as stale as yesterday's coffee. Ineu, find them.
textos.214: I've got them at home now, and I've already scolded them three times. Two more and maybe I'll let them out to play.
textos.215: Thank you, Ineu. I won't say it often, so listen carefully: thank you.
textos.216: Yes, Nelis. No, Nelis. Coming, Nelis.
textos.217: ...Oh, Ineu. It's you. Do what she says. She's always right. Always.
textos.218: Since the children came back, Nelis sings while she does the washing-up. Off-key, but she sings.
textos.219: Don't tell her I told you.
textos.220: Oh, son, have you seen that the tower clock has stopped? The altarpiece door that leads to the tower has been locked for years: since the clockmaker passed away, his widow, Carry, keeps the key, here at Our Lady's.
textos.221: Poor thing, she can't think straight: she's been looking for her dog, Pallofa, for two nights. If you find him and bring him to her, I'm sure she'll give you the key.
textos.222: Talk to her, but be patient: the poor thing hasn't been the same since the mist rose. She may need you.
textos.224: ★ You got a ROSARY BEAD: the light of the three sisters.
textos.225: Pallofa won't leave my side now. Thank you, Ineu. And don't forget the clock: without the hour, everything drags on.
textos.226: Pallofa! My Pallofa! Where did you get to, you little rascal? Look at you: skinnier than me and full of fleas.
textos.227: Thank you, Ineu, thank you. I have no money, but I owe you something. On those nights I saw, from my window, what no one should ever see.
textos.228: Huri, the little one from the right-hand door in Sant Benet, was the first. His bed was left empty and the window locked from the inside. He never went out alone at night: he was afraid of the dark.
textos.229: The next night it was Fram, the boy from the left-hand door. Pallofa barked at the mist, as if he saw someone I couldn't see, and went off after him. That's why I've been so frightened.
textos.230: My husband was the clockmaker, the one who looked after the clock. Since he passed, I've kept the tower key, and no one has been up there for years. Take it. That clock stopped at a quarter past three, and no one has noticed that time isn't passing any more.
textos.231: ★ You got the CLOCK TOWER KEY.
textos.232: Haven't you seen him yet? He's tiny, skinny and one-eyed, and he can't keep still. They say he wanders around Sant Antoni. Pick him up carefully: he's full of fleas.
textos.233: Oh, Ineu... no, you needn't worry about me. Well, yes. I'm looking for Pallofa, my dog.
textos.234: He's small and skinny, white with brown patches, and he's missing an eye: they say a cat ate it. He ran off two nights ago, after Fram, and hasn't come back.
textos.235: He likes to wander. If you find him, bring him back to me. I have no money, but I keep something at home that you might need.
textos.236: Pallofa doesn't run off any more: now there's no mist, he has nothing to chase.
textos.237: A small, skinny, one-eyed dog, full of fleas, looks at you with the only eye he has left. On his leather collar there's a tag: "PALLOFA".
textos.238: ★ You picked up PALLOFA. Take him to Carry.
textos.240: ← The Guesthouse and the Threshing Floor / → The arches of the Big House
textos.242: From inside comes a thread of accordion music, very faint... and a smell of frying.
textos.243: Psst! You're Ineu, aren't you? The monk who's asking about the children. Come in, quick, Càren's asleep and I don't want anyone to see us.
textos.244: I'm Eve. I do Càren's work, since she's been asleep ever since the mist came. I let you in for one reason: every night, when everything's shut, Brother Aleu knocks three times on the Gírgoles Door, and the door opens by itself. Inside, they say, there's another one made of iron, very old, that nobody has ever opened.
textos.245: And Iscu, Càren's son, has been sneaking off down the Disappearance path for two days: he says there's a gap between the trees "that grown-ups can't fit through". It wasn't the mist that took him, it was laziness: since his mother's been asleep, I wash the glasses and he vanishes. If you find him, tell him to come home for supper... and the washing-up.
textos.246: Sardi, on the other hand, comes every afternoon for bread and chocolate. Yesterday he didn't come.
textos.247: Iscu? I told you: he goes off down the Disappearance path, west of the Ruins, and hides through a gap between the trees "that grown-ups can't fit through". If you find him, tell him to come home for supper.
textos.248: This key... it's old iron, like the outer door, the Gírgoles Door! Did you find it in the Big House? The door is in the Gírgoles Hall: from the Cellar Yard, take the east path, between the trees.
textos.249: And the Pianist has taught you the song. Be careful in there.
textos.250: Before you go in, stop by the Sanctuary: the Pianist always says there's a song for every door.
textos.251: This sword shines as if it were happy. Maybe we could open the door with it... but the lock needs a key. A big iron key.
textos.252: Isílder says the monks hid everything in the Big House. Maybe the key too.
textos.253: I can't help you open the iron door: it has no lock for any key in the Tavern. They say the monks sealed it with a shining sword.
textos.254: Find that sword, Ineu. I'll stay here, pretending to work.
textos.255: Sardi's back here for his afternoon snack every day. Càren's still asleep, but she snores more happily.
textos.256: Shh... Galf? Ah, yes. He wants the ice crystal from the hermitage of Sant Gabriel, doesn't he? He's always longed to look at the sky.
textos.257: I was the sacristan there for many years, until I couldn't manage the steps any more. I've had the key in my pocket ever since: nobody's ever asked me for it.
textos.258: Here. But lock it properly, the lock is old. And don't take anything but the crystal.
textos.259: ★ You got the SANT GABRIEL KEY.
textos.260: Shh... keep your voice down, lad, I'm enjoying a frosted anisette. Eve made it for me, and you don't drink this: you savour it.
textos.261: A bit of ice, a splash of water, and let it do its work. Good things are never in a hurry. I know about waiting: I've been sitting at this table for sixty years.
textos.262: Since Càren fell asleep, Eve has run the tavern on her own and never complains. That's someone made of good stuff.
textos.263: Now hush, lad, my anisette's running out.
textos.264: Hey, wait. I've got something that might help you. One night I found a key on the ground: Brother Aleu had dropped it and didn't even notice.
textos.265: It's rusty, but it still turns. You can have it: I've got nothing to open. And you never saw me, right?
textos.268: Shh! Keep your voice down! If Eve finds me, she'll have me washing glasses till Christmas.
textos.269: My name's Iscu. I found the gap between the trees "that grown-ups can't fit through" and this hut. Nobody else knows about it: here nobody bosses me around!
textos.270: There was an old deck of cards on the table, and I love playing solitaire. Better than washing glasses!
textos.271: I could spend all day playing solitaire with these cards. And here, at least, there are no glasses to wash.
textos.272: My solitaire came out! I love cards. Now I don't need to hide so much...
textos.273: ← Disappearance Path / → Cemetery / ↑ Cells / ↓ The Cellar and the Square
textos.274: ← The Cellar (ping-pong) / → Gírgoles Hall / ↑ The Ruins / ↓ Square
textos.275: Hey, Ineu! The greatest challenge in the Miracle is beating Jusef and his magic serve. Do you dare?
textos.276: Mr Pomers plays with a stone paddle. Stone! And even so, he beats me easily.
textos.277: Easy, lad. You don't chase the ball, you wait for it.
textos.278: I play with a stone paddle. Stone, yes: it weighs as much as a brick and has no rubber or anything. When you play at the table, you won't see me or the paddle; there's no need.
textos.279: Because what you play with doesn't matter. The paddle is just an extension of the soul. What counts is the spirit of the game, the magic you carry inside.
textos.280: The table's yours whenever you like, lad. Want to try returning my serve again?
textos.281: Welcome to the Cellar, traveller. The paddles and the ball are only the bark: what I practise here is white magic.
textos.282: This is my magic serve. So far, nobody has managed to stop it.
textos.283: Want to try it? One game, first to seven.
textos.284: As you wish. The table isn't going anywhere.
textos.285: You've beaten me again, you've understood the magic of my serve perfectly. Any time you like, we'll play again.
textos.286: You've... you've beaten me... My magic serve, for the first time... You beat me fair and square.
textos.287: This is for you: Mamet's Lamp. Mamet was an old hermit of the Miracle who knew every underground passage and every crack in the walls.
textos.288: Its flame burns on an ancient oil that never goes out. In dark passages and in the gloom of old stones, its light will show you what seems hidden.
textos.290: And a secret, for someone who knows how to return a serve: that carriage wheel in the Cellar isn't decoration. Behind it is the monks' tunnel to the Big House. But it weighs as much as a loaded cart.
textos.291: Leaving already? The table won't run away. Come back whenever you like.
textos.292: As you wish. Come back any time: Július says the second time always goes better.
textos.293: (There's too much mist in the hole to see anything... I need a light.)
textos.294: (Mamet's Lamp pierces the darkness a little... There's a pale sheet hidden at the back!)
textos.296: A torn parchment (fragment 1 of 2): / "When the Birdcatcher was locked in his cage, a monk sealed the iron door with the light of the sword Runna and left it sleeping in the stone. Then he hid the key to the door where no one would find it. / The other half of this chronicle I leave under lock and key, in the church tabernacle."
textos.297: The parchment ends here, but it says the other half is under lock and key, in the church tabernacle. And every night, they say, a monk's shadow appears on this wall.
textos.298: The monk's shadow appeared when I read the parchment... Is it the monk of the seal? When I have the other fragment, Father Alberic will know how to read them together.
textos.300: For centuries I have heard no language but that of the stones. Only the song of the stones can wake me fully.
textos.301: The one who plays the organ knows it, and you already carry it in your tarota. Sing it to me here, little monk.
textos.302: The one who plays the organ knows it. Learn it, little monk, and come back to sing it to me here.
textos.303: Play the Vespers Song on the tarota.
textos.304: I was the one who closed the door. When they opened the cemetery, laughing, my brothers stopped resting and the seal cracked.
textos.305: Underground there is a cage, little monk, and something that has forgotten no song and no child. I can only keep watch. You can close it again.
textos.306: The sword sleeps to the south-east, among stones, where the sun comes to rest. Receive my word, which weighs nothing and cannot be seen, and remember: darkness fears light, but laughter even more.
textos.307: I can only tell you the words; Father Alberic will know how to understand them. When you call them out before the sword, my word will make it recognise you.
textos.308: Now I can rest in peace.
textos.310: Father Alberic, the plaque at the Dolmen says that only one who holds the permission of the sacred tree, the words of wisdom and the divine blessing can raise Runna. What does it mean?
textos.311: I have that in the Chronicle, son. Let me read it to you.
textos.312: "To raise the sword, three things are needed: the permission of the oldest tree, which sits at table with everyone; the words the monk left behind, which only one who has spoken with his shadow can understand; and the prior's blessing, which is God's blessing passed through human hands."
textos.313: The sacred tree is the Great Linden, the one by the cells: its medallion is the permission. The words are kept by the monk's shadow, in the Ruins, and only I will understand them when you tell me. And the divine blessing is Father Jòrdius's, the prior's.
textos.317: "With the light of Runna they closed the door, and with the same light they closed his tomb. While the crack gives off mist, the door is not fully shut."
textos.318: The tomb is in the Cemetery, behind the Sanctuary and the Monastery, and mist seeps from its crack. Until it's closed I can't read you the rest: the mist erases the words you'll need.
textos.319: You've spoken with the shadow, haven't you? I've suspected it for a while. In the Chronicle there's a margin I couldn't read: a faded word, in the same hand that wrote the fragments.
textos.320: With the word he gave you, now I understand. "Darkness fears light, but laughter even more." These are the words that awaken Runna, son: it isn't a spell, it's a truth. Say them before the sword, whole and with all your heart.
textos.321: And one more thing, son. Years ago, in the library, I found a secret compartment inside the oldest book of all, and in it was this: a stone medallion carved with an open book. It's hundreds of years old.
textos.322: I didn't know what it was for. Now I do: take it to the plaque at the Dolmen, and keep the words inside you for the moment you must say them.
textos.323: ★ You got the MEDALLION OF WISDOM!
textos.324: You know the words now, son. All that remains is for the day to come when you call them out.
textos.326: You've found both fragments! Let me read them... Yes. The Chronicle I keep in the library tells of it: a monk sealed the darkness with the light of the sword Runna.
textos.327: "Since the third church was left unfinished, the monk's shadow can be clearly seen on the wall of the Ruins: half bent over, hands joined, as if praying. It appears every night."
textos.328: The monk's shadow... It harms no one, Ineu. I believe it's the monk who sealed the darkness with the light of Runna. Go to the Ruins, past the Cellar Yard: it's on the wall of the unfinished church. Talk to it.
textos.329: Ineu, son. This mist isn't natural. The mists here come down from the mountains; this one rises from under the ground.
textos.330: They say a monk's shadow appears in the Ruins every night. There are two fragments of an old chronicle scattered around the Sanctuary: one in the Ruins and another in the church tabernacle. Bring them to me and we'll read them together.
textos.332: (The crack has closed and the mist no longer rises to the surface. Those who closed the door are at rest again.)
textos.333: (Without the mist that came out of here, the voice of the Man in the Cage no longer reaches so far, and the doors it used to open by itself won't open any more. But the mist that has already gathered underground, in the Gírgoles, is still trapped down there.)
textos.334: "The monks of the Miracle, of now and of old."
textos.335: This bouquet is from Brother Floresc, for the monks who sleep here. I'll leave it at the angel's feet.
textos.336: (The petals tremble, as if someone were breathing nearby. The angel, who was looking at the ground, lifts its face to the sky and smiles: it no longer weeps alone.)
textos.337: Brother Floresc will be pleased. He said that when I got back, he'd have something for me at Sant Antoni.
textos.338: ★ You left the BOUQUET OF FLOWERS at the angel's feet.
textos.340: "Here rest those who closed the door."
textos.341: Disappearance Path. / "Whoever follows the footsteps does not return alone."
textos.345: "The path keeps twelve words. Whoever listens to them will find the name of those who are silent."
textos.347: When the mist covers the Miracle, the footsteps of the absent will return with the dawn.
textos.348: I have it all now. These are words to be spoken aloud... before the altar.
textos.349: I only understand the words I noted down on the path. The signs I'm missing... are on the columns.
textos.350: "When the mist covers the Miracle, the footsteps of the absent will return with the dawn."
textos.352: The key to the Sanctuary's tabernacle! The monks left it here. With this I can open the tabernacle in the altarpiece.
textos.353: Rovellonera Wood. / "Whoever doesn't look at the ground gets lost. Saffron milk caps always grow beside the right path. If you go wrong, you'll return to the first clearing."
textos.354: ← Rovellonera / "Where there are milk caps, there are pines; where there are pines, there's a path."
textos.355: Mr Buidor's key fits the lock. The hermitage door opens.
textos.356: The hermitage of Sant Gabriel is locked.
textos.359: ↑ Hermitage of the Disappearance / → Guesthouse / ← Rovellonera
textos.360: Take a good look at the stars with the telescope, lad. The Reservoirs are the best lookout in the district... once you can get there.
textos.361: A real ice crystal! I've been looking for one for years. Give me a while.
textos.362: A telescope! With this you'll see things no monk has ever seen. So you don't lose your way: the stars mark the path.
textos.364: Mmm? Ah, a monk! Sit down, sit on the bench opposite, it's better for a chat.
textos.365: Come back when you have the ice crystal, lad. The Sant Gabriel hermitage opens with Mr Buidor's key.
textos.366: I've told you, lad: Mr Buidor has the hermitage key, at the Tavern. He was the sacristan. Ask him for it.
textos.367: That's better. I'm Galf, inventor. I live in the Sant Antoni cell, but I come here every day: it's the only spot where no roof hides the sky from me. I have ideas even I don't understand.
textos.368: If you bring me an ice crystal, I'll build you a telescope to look at the sky. There's one in the Sant Gabriel hermitage.
textos.369: But the hermitage is locked. The sacristan had the key, Mr Buidor, who retired years ago and now spends his days at the Tavern. Ask him for it on my behalf.
textos.370: From the telescope you can see the whole village, and tonight there isn't a wisp of mist.
textos.371: A small chest, so cold it hurts my hands. The lock is full of ice and gives way when I touch it. Carved on the lid: "The dew of dawn does not melt, even in summer."
textos.373: The last star has gone out above the eastern reservoir. There's a light in the water: I have to go there.
textos.374: (A three-legged stand, planted in the middle of the lookout. It seems made to hold something... a kind of tripod.)
textos.375: (Maybe the telescope Galf told me about would fit here. He needs to build it for me.)
textos.376: (Someone who knows about contraptions could tell what it's for. Galf, the inventor at the Threshing Floor, might know something.)
textos.377: They say that on St Lawrence's night the sky weeps. Count the tears... and maybe they'll show you something.
textos.378: ★ You got the TEAR OF ST LAWRENCE.
textos.379: It shines just like the seven stars... They say the mist doesn't dare touch the light of St Lawrence. The path to the Dolmen, to the east, is full of it.
textos.383: Look who it is! You've found me here too: from now on, whenever you like, I can take you to this place.
textos.384: Hey, monk! Galf built me this contraption: it runs on steam and never gets tired. If you need to go far, hop on: I can take you anywhere we've already met, and the more places you know me from, the farther we can go.
textos.385: So far I only know this place, monk. When you find me somewhere else, I'll take you there.
textos.386: Where to, monk? Pick one of the places where we've already met.
textos.387: Seven stars... and a bird escaping from an open cage. It's the night of the Tears of St Lawrence!
textos.388: I can't see a thing here. I'd need a light the mist couldn't put out...
textos.389: (Runna is on top of the slab. Maybe I can climb up from behind.)
textos.390: Only one who holds the permission of the sacred tree, the words of wisdom and the divine blessing may raise Runna.
textos.392: (I still need one more medallion to fill the plaque.)
textos.394: (The three medallions are still in place on the plaque. The sword is mine now: Runna.)
textos.395: (The permission of the sacred tree... the words of wisdom... the divine blessing. What can it all mean? Father Alberic must know: he'll have it written in the Chronicle.)
textos.397: (Some very low branches, thick as trunks, reach down to the ground and block the path. There's no way through here.)
textos.398: (They all face east, where the dawn rises, and in the distance there's a clearing with an enormous pine. If the pine listens to anyone, it must be from that side. I'll have to get there the other way: through Sant Antoni, maybe.)
textos.399: (In front of the pine, a low marker stone, worn and covered in moss. It's carved with a pine with three trunks and, below it, three notes.)
textos.400: Three branches has the old pine, / three songs it needs to hear. / One song for every branch: / only then the path is clear.
textos.401: (One song for every branch... I still need to learn one from the Pianist before I can try.)
textos.403: (Three songs, three branches. I'll try it with the tarota, right here.)
textos.404: (I'll need the tarota to answer it.)
textos.405: (Between two roots of the trunk there's a folded sheet of paper, kept like a treasure.)
textos.406: (Birds chirp among the branches and the pine stirs a little, as if breathing. It seems happy.)
textos.407: (An old pine, with three trunks spreading like three arms. It seems to be listening.)
textos.409: "To whoever hears this pine breathe again: /  / Before the mist, the birds slept in the pines of this wood. At dawn they all sang together, and that song brought the land to life: the Song of the Miracle."
textos.410: "One lonely man, the Birdcatcher, wanted it for himself. He locked the birds in a cage and took the song away. And with the song went the dawn, and the mist began."
textos.411: "There were two more songs, brothers of that one: the Song of Dawn, which drives the mist away, and the Vespers Song, which the earth listens to. They were afraid he would take them too, so they came to hide here, in the branches of this pine: one in each. Silent, like a child keeping a secret."
textos.412: "One afternoon, tired, I sat down beneath it. I listened to them and wrote them down in three sounds: one, two and three. They are the tarota's notes. Each note is one of the branches."
textos.413: "The pine lets through only one who carries the three songs, for only one who carries them can return them to the birds. When the mist has gone for good, let those who keep the stolen birds come here. This wood is their home. /  / — The Cortiner"
textos.414: (The roots have sunk into the earth like a long breath, and the birds have returned to the branches. The path from here to the Dolmen is clear.)
textos.415: Please don't run away. Everyone who sees me runs off. I just want to talk to someone.
textos.416: I came to pick milk caps with my mother. She always said: "Where there are milk caps, there are pines; where there are pines, there's a path." But I only looked at the milk caps, and I forgot the path.
textos.417: My mother had tied my braids with two pink ribbons. When I realised I was lost, I ran, and the ribbons fell somewhere in the wood. That was many, many years ago.
textos.418: I lost one on the Rovellonera path, and the other in a clearing in the middle of the Rovellonera wood. Without them I can't feel my mother's hands. If you could bring them to me...
textos.419: I'll find them. You won't be left alone, I promise.
textos.420: You have them... both of them? Oh, monk...
textos.421: I can feel them... it's my mother's hands tying them. Mother...?
textos.422: I've found you, my darling. Forgive me for taking so long.
textos.423: I'm not afraid any more. She's tied my braids, like before. Thank you, monk.
textos.424: The other ribbon is for you. Keep it: it protects those who get lost.
textos.426: It will take the first blow you receive in each new place. Now you won't be alone.
textos.427: Nor will you. You'll never be alone again.
textos.431: Thank you for taking me home, monk.
textos.432: Look at the doll! Fram sewed her head back on and says she's a brave doll now. And I'm not letting him go anywhere ever again!
textos.433: Fram's back! I don't have to wait alone by the door any more. Today we'll play all day!
textos.434: Don't touch her, all right? I pulled her head off because I was angry, and only Fram knows how to sew it back on.
textos.435: The doll is waiting. I'm waiting too.
textos.436: Zoooom! The doll flies above the clouds... and lands on the moon! Oops... a monk.
textos.437: Hello. I'm Ineu. What's your name?
textos.438: Mandu. And she's the doll. We always play here, by the door, waiting for Fram.
textos.440: Yes. We slept in the same room. One night I fell asleep with him beside me, and in the morning his bed was empty. He always tells me where he's going, and this time...
textos.441: Nelis says the mist took him. But I told him not to go! I told him! And he went anyway! WHY WON'T HE COME BACK?!
textos.442: That's enough! I'VE PULLED THE DOLL'S HEAD OFF! And I don't care: now Fram will have to come back and sew it on!
textos.443: Easy, Mandu. Let me see her: maybe I can sew it.
textos.444: No! Don't touch her! Only Fram knows how to sew dolls' heads: he fixes everything that gets broken.
textos.445: Then I'll find him and bring him back to you. And he'll sew up your doll.
textos.448: The angel's tomb has fresh flowers every day. I'm not the one who brings them... and don't ask me who.
textos.449: The gloves are a bit big on you, eh? You'll grow into them. Use them to move heavy things, not to push people around.
textos.450: You left them for the angel? God bless you, son. The monks of old must be pleased: someone still remembers them.
textos.451: Here. These are the old monks' stonemason's gloves: they lifted the stones of the Sanctuary with them. I no longer have the strength to use them, but you do.
textos.452: ★ You got the GLOVES OF POWER!
textos.453: They say that with them on, a boy can move a cartwheel as if it were made of cork. I've never seen it. But I'd never seen a mist like this one, either.
textos.454: The bouquet goes on the tomb of the stone angel, on the right side of the Cemetery, son. Behind the Monastery, up the path. And watch out for the critters.
textos.455: Ineu... Good morning, son. Are they letting you grow up at last?
textos.456: Forgive me for walking slowly: these knees are older than the clock tower.
textos.457: I live in the Monastery, but every morning I walk down to Sant Antoni. Huri, the boy from Sant Benet, used to come and steal my figs and I'd pretend not to see him. For two days now the fig tree has been full.
textos.458: Every week I take flowers to the angel in the Cemetery, for the monks who sleep there. But with this mist I can't get there: my legs won't obey me and the critters show me no respect.
textos.459: Would you do me a favour? Leave this bouquet at the angel's feet. And come back, I have something for you.
textos.460: ★ You got a BOUQUET OF FLOWERS.
textos.461: Put it to good use, monk! And watch out, stone things don't always stay still.
textos.462: Hey, monk! I'm Gori from the Hut. I know every shortcut in the Miracle, and tools even better.
textos.463: Good to know. For now I was just stopping by to say hello.
textos.464: Well, now you know where to find me if you ever need a hand.
textos.465: The hut is right next door: climb the ladder. In my toy chest, the crank is at the bottom. Don't tire your arm out!
textos.466: Hey, monk! I'm Gori from the Hut. I know every shortcut in the Miracle, and tools even better.
textos.467: Gori, they tell me you know about tools. There's an old iron wheel with no crank, and without one there's no way to turn it.
textos.468: A crank! I've got an iron one, a good one. It fits well wheels, presses... and, if need be, the wheel of a stubborn statue.
textos.469: But I hid it up in my hut, the one raised on stilts, in my toy chest. Nobody dares touch my toys, because I never let anyone lay a finger on them. NEVER! NEVER!
textos.470: But you've come for something serious, so just this once I'll let you. Climb the ladder, the door isn't locked, and take it.
textos.471: A big book, open on the table, in a monk's handwriting. At the top of the page it says: "On the punishment of the cellarer brother".
textos.472: "The cellarer brother drank the sacristy wine, barrel after barrel, and then swore it had evaporated."
textos.473: "When we found out, the Prior did not cast him out: he had him turned to stone and set him to guard the crypt until the wine turns to vinegar. In the crypt it never turns to vinegar."
textos.474: "That's why they call him the Grape Man. He sleeps facing the wall, like a child being punished, and only wakes if someone turns him round and looks him in the face."
textos.475: It isn't mine... Better ask Gori before taking it.
textos.477: The mechanism is on the wooden frame on the left: three gears in positions I, II and III. Each time I touch one it changes size: small, medium, large.
textos.478: "Clockmaker's note. The clock only runs if the gears are in order: the small one first, the medium in the middle, and the large one at the back."
textos.479: (It's ticking again! Now the whole village will hear it.)
textos.480: Nobody has opened this for generations. There must be another way in.
textos.481: (The bar's off: now I can come and go through the square.)
textos.482: His head is on backwards. He seems to be watching something behind him.
textos.483: The statue's head is turned right round, facing the wall. At the base of the pedestal there's an iron wheel with gears, but it's missing the crank needed to turn it.
textos.484: The mist... has woken me. So many years staring at the wall, and now they let me go. Someone will pay for it.
textos.485: It moved! The purple mist has brought it to life!
textos.486: You want the crypt? Neither you nor anyone else will get past. I'll crush you like grapes.
textos.487: If this wakes the stone guardian, I won't be able to withstand his mace bare-handed. I'll need to come back with a weapon.
textos.488: The mist is leaving... I can feel the stone again. So this is how it ends: centuries guarding what they never cared to look at.
textos.489: They left me here, and your Man in the Cage only woke me so that I'd be killed.
textos.490: Go down, if you like. Down there no one will forgive you, just as no one forgave me.
textos.491: I'm going back to my pedestal. It's all they left me.
textos.492: The Grape Man rests for ever.
textos.494: (Now he's looking straight at me. I don't like it one bit.)
textos.496: (The slab has no lock or handle. The pulley chain is tied to it: the mechanism on the floor must raise it.)
textos.497: (A stone slab with no lock or handle. It won't budge: it has to be opened some other way.)
textos.498: ← The Tavern and the Guesthouse / → Sanctuary Square
textos.499: The Linden supper, eh? People only think about the food and forget the flowers. I've been putting flowers there since I was young.
textos.500: The moon flowers are for those who are missing. Put them in the middle of the table; I'll come and sit there too.
textos.502: I heard the Guesthouse door opening. It's them, isn't it? Dolòria, Pilària, Carmèlia... the priestesses of our house.
textos.503: Three nights locked up twenty paces from me, and me here with my flowers, knowing nothing. Their prayer has always kept the peace in this land.
textos.504: And Sardi... my son Sardi. He's seven, monk. Every afternoon he'd climb the plum tree and stuff himself with plums until he couldn't say a word. If you find him, tell him his father hasn't stopped watering the plum tree.
textos.505: The moon flower has bloomed on the slab. I'll never stop tending it.
textos.506: Isílder, look what I've got. Rosansa gave it to me: she says it's a Moon Seed.
textos.507: A Moon Seed! I haven't seen one in thirty years. It blooms at night, by the light of the moon, and only if it's planted by someone who hasn't lost hope.
textos.508: My Sardi used to sit here waiting for them to open, and he said moon flowers sing when they bloom. Give it to me, monk: I can still dig a hole. And watch closely.
textos.509: The slab has moved aside... Beneath it is the path the monks used to carry food to the cells in the house's cellar. No one has set foot on it for centuries.
textos.510: Go down carefully, son. And if you find my Sardi... tell him the moon flowers have opened again.
textos.512: The slab still lights up with your sword's glow. You know what to do: Rosansa, at the cells, and that strange seed she carries in her cart.
textos.513: Don't be surprised to see me here every day, rain or shine. Sardi looked after this garden so well. Since the mist took him, I tend it so that when he comes back, he'll find everything just as he left it.
textos.514: Have you noticed the slab? No man has ever been able to move it. They say it only responds to the light of a moon seed. The only person I can think of who might have seen one is the vegetable seller who comes round the cells now and then. You could try.
textos.515: Monk, wait! Look at the slab: it's lit up. I've seen it every day for years and it's never done anything like that.
textos.516: It must be Runna. The slab glows in time with the sword.
textos.517: This pale, bluish light... I remember one like it: the light moon seeds give off when they bloom at night. Maybe a moon flower would help the slab understand what you're asking of it.
textos.518: There are no moon seeds left. But Rosansa, the vegetable seller, has come by the cells again, and for years she's carried a strange seed in her cart that nobody can identify. Ask her.
textos.519: The moon flowers open in the daytime now. I'd say it's the children's laughter that fools them.
textos.520: A stone slab carved with a cross. The Moon Seed would want soil nearby, but it needs someone who knows the garden: Isílder.
textos.521: A stone slab carved with a cross, set firmly in the ground. Isílder says the vegetable seller might have the seed needed to open it.
textos.522: A stone slab carved with a cross, set firmly in the ground. It won't move an inch, but there must be some way to open it. Maybe the man by the pergola, Isílder, can help us.
textos.523: The Guesthouse / → The Tavern / ← The Threshing Floor
textos.524: Fresh vegetables, local fruit! Onions, radishes, cabbages... What can I get you, monk?
textos.525: Nothing to eat, thanks. I'm looking for a seed: a moon flower seed, for the slab in the Guesthouse garden.
textos.526: A moon flower? Mmm... I've had a strange seed at the bottom of my cart for years, among the onions. Nobody knows what it is, not even me.
textos.527: Here, it's yours. May it bloom for whoever knows how to care for it.
textos.529: I must be off now, I've still got three villages to get to today. Goodbye, monk!
textos.530: And the slab in the Guesthouse garden? It's the old monks' work: they sealed it with the same light of Runna that sealed the iron door. Now that the sword is awake, the stone answers its light again.
textos.531: And the slab in the Guesthouse garden? It's the old monks' work: they sealed it with the same light of Runna that sealed the iron door. As long as the sword sleeps, the slab will sleep with it.
textos.532: Come in, son: this house is yours again.
textos.533: The door is locked from the inside.
textos.537: Some light music, three notes, might wake her.
textos.538: Oh, young monk! What a lovely song... I haven't heard it like that in sixty years. I'm Dolòria.
textos.539: The mist came in through the cellar three nights ago. I saw a brother in a habit, whistling like the birds, carrying Sardi off into the mist and laughing softly.
textos.540: If you pass through the garden, say hello to Isílder, this house's gardener. A good man, heartbroken since the little ones disappeared.
textos.541: Carmèlia, our high priestess, is locked in the chapel at the back. Black brambles cover her door: the kind not even a sickle can cut. They say they only yield to a sword of light. That sword you carry, son, shines like the one they speak of. Try it.
textos.542: Carmèlia, our high priestess, is locked in the chapel at the back. Black brambles cover her door: the kind not even a sickle can cut. They say they only yield to a sword of light.
textos.543: Be careful, son. Between the three of us sisters we keep this house's Shelter. When all three of us are free, it will be yours.
textos.544: Go with God, son. The chair hurts my bones, but my ears still work fine.
textos.545: Sardi is stealing biscuits from the pantry again. A sure sign he's completely well.
textos.546: At last! Three nights I've been banging on this door! I'm Pilària, and no, I haven't sat still for a single minute.
textos.547: I'm telling you because I saw it: Brother Aleu, that pest who was always playing with the children, went to the Gírgoles Door many nights, and the door opened by itself for him, as if the mist obeyed him. I never trusted that smile of his.
textos.548: All those innocent children stolen by this cursed mist... Find them, monk! Save them all!
textos.549: Thank you for your courage! May your strength never fail you!
textos.550: If you need someone who keeps her eyes wide open, you know where to find me.
textos.551: We've put a candle for you in every room, Ineu. And another just in case.
textos.552: Welcome, child of God. I am Carmèlia, the high priestess of this house. We had lost hope, but not prayer.
textos.553: The children of this land have been dragged into the darkness of a deep abyss. The night the mist shut us in our rooms, their beds were left empty. Save them, son: bring all the stolen children home.
textos.554: In the books of this house I have read that the Birdcatcher stole the birds' song, and that only that same song can open his cage. The one you learned from the Pianist, son, is the one he stole. Don't let it go.
textos.555: In the books of this house I have read that the Birdcatcher stole the birds' song, and that only that same song can open his cage. You will learn it: the Pianist remembers it.
textos.556: May patience go with you, son.
textos.557: May the light of the Miracle go with you, son.
textos.558: All three of us owe you one. And we always pay our debts... in cakes.
textos.559: "For the one who brought light back to this house. At the bottom of the Gírgoles, before you reach the cage, there is a burning mist: our shelter will clear it as you pass." — Dolòria, Pilària and Carmèlia
textos.560: ★ You got the SISTERS' SHELTER: it protects you from the poisonous mist blocking the way to the Cage Hall.
textos.561: (Locked. It used to open by itself for Aleu because the mist coming out of the tomb obeyed the Master's voice... but the tomb is sealed and the mist no longer rises: now the door opens for no one. I need the monks' key.)
textos.562: (Locked. They say it opens by itself for Aleu: the mist obeys him. Not me.)
textos.565: (This is where it all comes from. I'm missing the sword that sealed it... and a key.)
textos.566: (The Iron Key won't go in: this lock is much smaller. Brother Aleu must have another one.)
textos.567: (Someone must have seen him going there at night... Iscu, Càren's son! Eve said he sneaks off down the Disappearance path, through a gap in the trees.)
textos.569: "The mushrooms of the cave sing together or fall silent together. Touch one and you'll wake the two beside it too. When they all sing, the way will open."
textos.573: (The stone blocks are asleep. Maybe the tarota can wake them.)
textos.575: (The bars have no lock. Only a song can open them: the Song of the Miracle.)
textos.576: I'm all right, Ineu. The mist is good company once it stops asking for anything.
textos.577: Come back whenever you like. If my heart ever turns, I'll find someone to keep me company...
textos.578: Not yet, lad. Let me hear them laugh.
textos.580: The Master is coming, monk. Can you hear him yet?
textos.581: Ineu! I dreamed I was a bird in a cage... and now I just want to laugh!
textos.582: Where's the bird man? Did you chase him off? Ha ha ha! You should have seen his face!
textos.583: Dad must be worried, watering the plum tree... Shall we go home, Ineu?
textos.584: (This mist burns my throat... Without the Shelter of the Guesthouse priestesses I won't be able to get through.)
textos.585: (An invisible force won't let me through. Without the Song of the Miracle, the bars won't listen to me. The Pianist at the Sanctuary has to teach it to me.)
textos.586: (The Man in the Cage is whistling louder than the song.)
textos.587: Again, monk? The Master never tires.
textos.588: Come back in, little one. Laughter always comes back.
textos.590: (Three cocoons of mist, hanging like sausages... Huri, Fram, Sardi. They're asleep.)
textos.592: Silence! No one raises their voice here, monk. The Master sleeps, and I watch over his sleep.
textos.593: Brother Aleu, it's me. Lower your voice.
textos.594: For every laugh I bring him, he rewards me with a "good lad, Aleu". You can't understand what it means to me that someone so powerful knows my name.
textos.595: You've always had everyone's favour, you spoilt brat!
textos.596: That isn't admiring someone, Aleu, it's caging yourself.
textos.597: Too late, far too late! Master! MASTER, he's here! The monk who wants to take the children from you!
textos.598: Aleu, my son, there's no need to shout.
textos.599: A young monk's feet upon my stone.
textos.600: Let the children go back to their families!
textos.601: A child laughing... I haven't heard one for centuries.
textos.602: The cage is full of stolen laughter. There's still room for yours.
textos.603: You already know Runna. And now you'll know me!
textos.604: Runna... Such a small sword for such a large hall.
textos.605: Leave him to me, Master, this time I'll crush him!
textos.606: Stand aside, Aleu. Tonight the Master himself will show you how it's done.
textos.609: So much laughter, and none of it was for me.
textos.611: Brother Aleu, the cage will open. You can come with us.
textos.613: His voice spoke inside my head every night. It was the only one that ever spoke to me.
textos.614: Listen to them, they're laughing so loudly no cage could hold them.
textos.615: Come with us, Aleu. There's room for everyone at the refectory table.
textos.616: I know there is. Thank you, Ineu.
textos.617: The Master is in there... Someone has to watch over him. Someone who knows what it's like not to be seen.
textos.621: Huri, we never doubted for a moment that Ineu would save you. His destiny was written in the chronicle of the Miracle.
textos.622: Mandu! What happened to the doll? Give her here, only I know how to sew dolls' heads.
textos.623: Thank you, Fram! She's got her head back... and you'll never go away again, will you?
textos.624: Fram! You're back! And you'll never go away again, will you?
textos.626: Sardi! My boy... Three nights without a word of you.
textos.627: Dad! Did you water the plum tree?
textos.628: Every day, son. Every day. So that when you came back, you'd find everything just as you left it.
textos.629: I'm not washing a single glass today! Big celebration: the children are home!
textos.630: Today, fine. Tomorrow I'll save you the whole sinkful.
textos.631: Now, yes. Ineu, the tarota: today you start the Song of the Miracle, and the organ will follow you.
textos.632: Mother and I heard it from far away. You play very well, monk.
textos.633: Thank you for taking me home.
textos.634: Can you hear the clock tower, Ineu? It's striking the hours again! For three nights time stood still, and you're the one who set it going again.
textos.635: My husband would be proud that the ticking of his clock brings us all together. Thank you, son.
textos.636: Father Jòrdius... Brother Aleu hasn't come back. He chose to stay with the Master, underground, and the cage swallowed him.
textos.638: When a man seeks admiration in the darkness because he cannot find love among his brothers, he ends up as his own jailer.
textos.639: He will have to answer before God and before us for every one of the children's tears. But the cage he himself chose to close... is where his mist will harm no one ever again.
textos.640: Now look around you, Ineu: the children are laughing and the Sanctuary is singing. Don't let his sorrow steal the light you've brought back to the Miracle. Welcome home, son.
textos.641: Today everyone is singing, even if the organ hits a sour note.
textos.643: The shepherds are listening, but this doesn't remind them of home. An ancient song, one for the cowbells: the Vespers Song.
textos.644: The shepherds are listening, but this doesn't remind them of home. It would have to be an older song: maybe the Pianist knows one.
textos.645: The shepherds listen in silence... It isn't time yet: first I need to speak to the Linden.
textos.646: The shepherds are smiling: music has come back here.
textos.647: The door to the right of the altarpiece is open now.
textos.648: It's too dark... I can only see one step ahead. Jusef, in the Cellar, kept a light.
textos.649: The mushrooms are singing: the mycelium is falling apart!
textos.650: The stone owl won't budge an inch. I need to be much stronger to move it.
textos.652: It's too heavy... it needs stronger hands.
textos.657: Not now: there are beasts nearby.
textos.659: A child's toy chest. It isn't mine: better not rummage through it.
textos.660: The Tear of St Lawrence shines like the stars. They say the mist doesn't dare touch it... Let's try.
textos.661: It worked! The light of the Tear has dispelled the mist: the path to the Dolmen is clear.
textos.662: Gori from the Hut is sure to lend me one, he's an expert in all kinds of tools.
textos.663: And another thing, son: the priestesses of the Guesthouse keep a Shelter against burning mists: don't go down to the depths without it.
textos.667: (I have the key, the Song of the Miracle and the Shelter: the two trials Father Alberic's Chronicle spoke of. Onward.)
textos.673: Once inside, there are two more trials: the burning mist, which only someone carrying the Shelter of the Guesthouse priestesses can cross (Brother Floresc's gloves will help you earn it), and the cage, whose bars only listen to the Song of the Miracle. Don't go down without all of it.
textos.674: And one more thing, son, not from the Chronicle but from a friend. Father Xèvius, the keeper of the Gírgoles door, I've known for forty years: he isn't bad, just once bitten. Thirty years ago Aleu fooled him with sweet words, and since then he trusts nobody. Understand him, and don't take it badly.
textos.675: He won't let you pass without proof of goodwill, and nothing convinces him like the Cortiner's Letter, which rests in the trunk of the Pine of the Three Songs. You'll have to wake the pine with the three songs: Dawn, Vespers and Miracle. Do it before you go to the door, because after that there's no turning back.
textos.676: Go through, son, go through. May the light of Runna go with you: down there you'll truly need it.
textos.677: Halt, lad. You shall not pass. Thirty years ago a kind-faced monk knocked on this door, said three sweet words... and my predecessor let him in.
textos.678: Since then, whoever wants to pass must prove their goodwill to me. Not with words, son: with deeds.
textos.679: (What proof can I show him? Maybe Father Alberic, in the Library, knows: it must be in the Chronicle.)
textos.680: Father Xèvius, I've brought this: the Cortiner's Letter. It was in the trunk of the Pine of the Three Songs. The birds have come back.
textos.681: The Cortiner's handwriting... and the blue seal, unbroken. Only someone who brings the birds back to the pine has a heart like that.
textos.682: Forgive me, son. Bad experiences leave wounds. Keep your eyes open down there: Aleu isn't who he used to be.
textos.685: The tomb, son. As long as the crack in the Cemetery gives off mist, I can't read you the rest of the Chronicle. Strike it with Runna and come back.
textos.686: Father Alberic, I have Runna now. So what else does the Chronicle say?
textos.687: Let me look at it once more.
textos.688: Strike the crack with Runna, son, and come back to see me.
textos.689: Father Alberic, I've sealed the tomb with Runna: the mist no longer rises.
textos.690: You've done well, son. With the light of Runna they closed the door, and with the same light, the tomb. Now I can tell you the rest.
textos.691: (The path is easier now: I just have to follow the milk caps. I don't need to remember the clues any more.)
textos.694: The priestesses' Shelter wraps me in a warm light, and the burning mist draws back before it. I can get through.
textos.695: Oh, mother of God, the shepherds' cowbells! I haven't heard them ring in twenty years. Let me play them for a moment...
textos.696: They carry an ancient music. With the tarota, the old songs can still wake what sleeps beneath the mist. Be careful: with this power, the mist won't forgive you.
textos.697: Good game, monk. But the serve is still mine.
textos.698: If you like, I'll ease off my serve a bit: the ball will go slower and you'll have more time. What do you say?
textos.700: By the way, you look pale. Would you like a glass of warm milk?
textos.701: By the way, would you like a glass of warm milk?
textos.702: Here. You've got more colour now. Enjoy, monk.
textos.705: The mist is gone for good, monk. Before I take to the road again, let me open the last cage.
textos.706: In it I carry the birds I rescued and have looked after for a long time. With the mist they wouldn't sing, but now they can fly free again.
textos.707: Now they can sing. Thank you for giving them back their song.
textos.708: Off you go home, Ineu: the Miracle will always remember its hero.
textos.709: And when you have Runna, come back to see me: there are pages of the Chronicle I can't read you yet.
textos.710: The tomb, son. A seal won't hold unless time holds it up: get the clock tower ticking again and strike the crack in the Cemetery with Runna. While it gives off mist I can't read you the rest of the Chronicle.
textos.711: One moment, son. Notice something: the tomb cracked at a quarter past three. That's the exact time the clock tower stopped.
textos.712: And you've already got it ticking: a good sign. A seal only holds if time holds it up.
textos.713: A seal won't hold unless time holds it up. First the clock has to tick again: Carry keeps the key to the altarpiece door, at Our Lady's.
textos.714: When the clock is ticking, strike the crack with Runna, son, and come back to see me.
textos.715: (The light won't give way. Something's missing... maybe it isn't yet... the hour.)
textos.716: A song the stones understand? Oh, son... Maybe it's the Vespers Song: it's very old, my mother taught it to me. Come, listen.

A bouquet wrapped in a scrap of parchment.

interficie.Rosa i descolorit. És de la Nena de les: Pink and faded. It belongs to the Girl with the Braids.
interficie.Un antic llum d'oli d'un vell ermità del: An old oil lamp that belonged to an old hermit of the Miracle. Its clear flame reveals secrets hidden in the dark and in cracks in the stone.
For watching the stars at the Reservoirs.
interficie.Una gota de llum caiguda del cel, de la: A drop of light fallen from the sky, on the night the sky weeps.
interficie.Del Germà Floresc, per a la tomba de l'à: From Brother Floresc, for the angel's tomb.
For moving things that are too heavy.
interficie.De ferro: encaixa en volants i rodes vel: Iron: it fits old wheels and handwheels.
interficie.Petita, amb un ocell gravat. Al Germà Al: Small, engraved with a bird. Brother Aleu dropped it; Iscu gave it to you.
interficie.La meitat d'un pergamí esquinçat, trobad: Half of a torn parchment, found in the Ruins.
interficie.L'altra meitat de la crònica, trobada al: The other half of the chronicle, found in the church tabernacle.
interficie.«El germà bodeguer es bevia el vi de la: "The cellarer brother drank the sacristy wine. We turned him to stone to guard the crypt until the wine turns to vinegar (in the crypt it never does). He sleeps facing the wall and only wakes if you look him in the face."
interficie.La va deixar al tronc del Pi dels Tres C: He left it in the trunk of the Pine of the Three Songs: it explains where the three songs came from and what they need to return to the birds.
interficie.Te l'ha donada el senyor Buidor, que va: Mr Buidor, who used to be the sacristan, gave it to you. It opens the Sant Gabriel hermitage.
interficie.De la Rosansa. L'Isílder sap on plantar-: From Rosansa. Isílder knows where to plant it.

The Bishop's Fountain, which they say could heal anyone, has fallen asleep. It's in Sant Joan Wood, in the north-west of the map. Worth going to have a look.
interficie.Ja tens totes les ofrenes: torna a la Fo: You have all the offerings: go back to the Bishop's Fountain.
interficie.A la Font del Bisbe, les ofrenes que fal: For the Bishop's Fountain, the missing offerings ({0}/3): St John's wort (in this very wood), rialla (a plant: in the Wood of the Pine of the Three Songs, south of Sant Antoni, guarded by poisonous mushrooms) and a plum from the Guesthouse Plum Tree.
interficie.Ja tens l'aigua de la Font del Bisbe. L': You have the water from the Bishop's Fountain. The Hollow Oak in the wood might know what to do with it.
interficie.A l'altra banda de l'Alzina Buida hi ha: On the other side of the Hollow Oak there's a gift for the path to the Linden.
interficie.Una boira espessa tapa un camí de les Ce: A thick mist blocks a path by the Cells. A brew would clear it.
interficie.El camí de la boira ja és clar. Al capda: The misty path is clear now. At the very top there's a tree that knows what to do about the critters waking up.
interficie.Al peu del Til·ler ha caigut alguna cosa: Something has fallen at the foot of the Linden that would serve you better than the pilgrim's staff.
At the Linden, some roots block the way. They're wood: maybe they'd give way to blows from a friendly branch.
interficie.A la pastura de la Cirosa, el Germà Aleu: In the Cirosa pasture, Brother Aleu has let the mist take him over: now he's the Shepherd of the Mist.
interficie.El pastor vell, vora el foc de la Cirosa: The old shepherd, by the fire in the Cirosa, keeps his grandparents' cowbells.
